## 7. The bit budget: keys deserve the bits

The theory says key damage carries an amplification factor and value damage does
not. Encode that in the simplest first-order model.

**Definition 7.1 (damage model).** For an amplification factor $A > 0$ and bit
widths $b_K, b_V \in \mathbb{N}$,
$$D_A(b_K, b_V) \;=\; \frac{A}{2^{b_K}} \;+\; \frac{1}{2^{b_V}} .$$

All arithmetic below is exact rational arithmetic; no floating point or rounding
is involved.

**Theorem 7.2 (move a bit to the keys).** If $2^{b_K} < A \cdot 2^{b_V}$ then
$$D_A(b_K + 1, b_V) \;<\; D_A(b_K, b_V + 1) .$$

*Proof.* A direct computation gives
$$D_A(b_K, b_V+1) - D_A(b_K+1, b_V) = \frac{A\,2^{b_V} - 2^{b_K}}{2^{b_K}\,2^{b_V+1}},$$
whose numerator is positive by hypothesis and whose denominator is positive.
$\square$

**Theorem 7.3 (equilibrium).** If $A\cdot 2^{b_V} \le 2^{b_K}$ then
$$D_A(b_K, b_V + 1) \;\le\; D_A(b_K + 1, b_V),$$
so a further transfer to the keys does not help.

*Proof.* The same identity with the sign reversed. $\square$

Theorems 7.2 and 7.3 together characterise the optimum exactly: **transfer bits
to the keys until the amplified key term balances the value term**, i.e. until
$2^{b_K} \approx A\,2^{b_V}$.

**Theorem 7.4 ($K8/V4$ is the unique optimum at $A = 16$ and a 12-bit budget).**
For all $b_K + b_V = 12$ with $b_K \ne 8$,
$$D_{16}(8,4) \;<\; D_{16}(b_K, b_V) .$$

*Proof.* Substituting $b_V = 12 - b_K$ gives
$D_{16}(b, 12-b) = 2^{4-b} + 2^{b-12}$, a strictly convex function of $b$
minimised where the exponents coincide, i.e. $4 - b = b - 12$, i.e. $b = 8$,
with value $2^{-4} + 2^{-4} = 1/8$. Finitely many cases $b = 0,\dots,12$ verify
the strict inequality. $\square$

**Corollary 7.5 (role split beats uniform split at equal bit rate).**
$$D_{16}(8,4) = \tfrac{1}{8} \;<\; \tfrac{17}{64} = D_{16}(6,6),$$
so at the same average of six bits per cache element, $K8/V4$ is better than
$K6/V6$ by more than a factor of two.

**Corollary 7.6 (the reversed split is far worse).**
$$8\,D_{16}(8,4) = 1 \;<\; \tfrac{257}{256} = D_{16}(4,8),$$
so spending the bits on the values costs more than eight times the guaranteed
damage.

Note that $A = 16$ here is a conservative stand-in for the *proved* amplification
$\|q\|_1$; a larger $A$ moves the optimum further toward the keys, never away.

---

## 8. How many key bits? A margin criterion

The worst-case results of Section 4 leave open the operational question: what
bit width is actually safe? The right variable is not the error norm but the
*decision margin*, because what a quantised key cache destroys is a
selection.

**Lemma 8.1 (margin certificate).** If $i$ is the strict top of $s$ with
$s_i - s_j > 2\varepsilon$ for all $j \ne i$, and $|s_j - s'_j| \le \varepsilon$
for all $j$, then $i$ is the strict top of $s'$.

*Proof.* For $j \ne i$: $s'_i \ge s_i - \varepsilon > s_j + \varepsilon \ge s'_j$. $\square$

**Theorem 8.2 (margin criterion for key bit width).** Suppose every key entry is
stored to resolution $\mathrm{res}(R,b) = R/2^b$, and the exact logit margin of
decision $i$ satisfies
$$s_i - s_j \;>\; 2\,\|q\|_1\,\frac{R}{2^{b}} \qquad \text{for all } j \ne i .$$
Then the quantised cache makes the same decision: $i$ is a strict top of the
quantised scores.

*Proof.* Combine Theorem 4.1 (each logit moves by at most
$\|q\|_1\mathrm{res}(R,b)$) with Lemma 8.1. $\square$

**Corollary 8.3 (bit count).** $b$ key bits suffice for all decisions of margin
at least $m$ as soon as
$$2^{b} \;>\; \frac{2\,\|q\|_1 R}{m}.$$

The requirement on $b$ is **logarithmic** in the amplification $\|q\|_1 R/m$:
each extra key bit doubles the query norm (or halves the margin) that can be
tolerated. This is why the cliff is a *threshold in bits* rather than a smooth
degradation, and why 8 is a plausible frontier while 4 is not.

**Proposition 8.4 (eight bits are safe at the reference scale).** At
$\|q\|_1 = 64$, $R = 1$, $m = 1$:
$$2 \cdot 64 \cdot \mathrm{res}(1,8) = \frac{128}{256} = \tfrac12 \;<\; 1 = m,$$
a factor-two cushion.

**Proposition 8.5 (four bits violate the criterion).** At the same scale,
$2 \cdot 64 \cdot \mathrm{res}(1,4) = 128/16 = 8 \not< 2$, so the criterion fails
even for a decision of margin $2$.

**Theorem 8.6 (four bits provably destroy a decision).** At the reference scale
there is an explicit two-position cache exhibiting the failure, not merely the
loss of the certificate: take $d = 1$, $q = 64$, exact keys $k = (1/32, 0)$ and
quantised keys $k' = (0,0)$. Then $\|q\|_1 = 64$; the per-entry error is
$1/32 \le \mathrm{res}(1,4) = 1/16$; the exact scores are $(2,0)$, so position
$0$ is a strict top with margin exactly $2$; and the quantised scores are
$(0,0)$, which have **no** strict top at all. The softmax is handed a tie and
the decision is gone.

Theorem 8.6 and Proposition 8.4 bracket the deployment rule from both sides:
**keys $\ge 8$ bits, values may take $4$.**

**Theorem 8.7 (no rescue by rescaling).** Let $c > 0$, and rescale keys by $c$
and the query by $1/c$. Then:
1. the logits are unchanged, $S(q/c,\; c\,k) = S(q, k)$, hence so is the entire
   attention output;
2. the key range scales to $cR$, since $|c\,k_{i,t}| \le cR$ whenever
   $|k_{i,t}| \le R$;
3. the governing amplification is invariant:
   $$\|q/c\|_1 \cdot \mathrm{res}(cR, b) \;=\; \|q\|_1 \cdot \mathrm{res}(R,b).$$

*Proof.* (1) $\sum_t (q_t/c)(c\,k_{i,t}) = \sum_t q_t k_{i,t}$. (2)
$|c\,k_{i,t}| = c|k_{i,t}| \le cR$. (3) $\|q/c\|_1 = \|q\|_1/c$ and
$\mathrm{res}(cR,b) = c\,\mathrm{res}(R,b)$; the factors $c$ cancel. $\square$

So the quantity that decides whether a key bit width is safe is a genuine
invariant of the attention configuration. **No normalisation scheme, no
per-channel scaling, no reparametrisation of the key space can buy a key bit.**
Whatever a normalisation scheme gains in key range, it loses in query norm.

---

## 9. Algorithms

Three procedures follow directly from the theory and are cheap enough to run
inside a serving stack.

**Algorithm A — Role-split bit allocation.** Given a total per-element budget
$T = b_K + b_V$ and an amplification estimate $A$, return the split minimising
$D_A$. By Theorems 7.2 and 7.3 the objective $2^{\log_2 A - b} + 2^{b - T}$ is
strictly convex in $b_K = b$, so a single sweep over $b = 0,\dots,T$ (or the
closed form $b^{*} = \mathrm{round}((T + \log_2 A)/2)$ followed by a comparison of
the two neighbouring integers) is exact. Complexity $O(T)$.

**Algorithm B — Safe key bit width from a margin distribution.** Given
$\|q\|_1$, key range $R$ and a target margin quantile $m$, return the least $b$
with $2^b > 2\|q\|_1 R / m$, i.e. $b = \lfloor \log_2(2\|q\|_1 R/m)\rfloor + 1$.
By Theorem 8.2 this bit width preserves every decision of margin at least $m$.
Complexity $O(1)$; estimating $m$ from a calibration set is $O(\text{tokens})$.

**Algorithm C — Codebook-collision audit.** Given a candidate key quantiser $Q$
as a black box and a probe budget $N$, evaluate $Q$ on the $N+1$ probes $i/N$
and search for a collision. Theorem 4.8 guarantees one exists whenever the
codebook has at most $N$ entries, and returns with it the explicit adversarial
query $2/(a-b)$ and a certified read-out gap of at least $1/4$. Complexity
$O(N)$ evaluations plus $O(N)$ hashing. This turns "is this new 4-bit key format
safe?" into a terminating computation whose answer is always no.

---

## 10. Discussion and honest limits

**What the theorems do and do not claim.** They are statements about the
attention functional: a convex combination on the value side, an inner product
followed by an exponential selection on the key side. They therefore apply to
any implementation. They are worst-case statements over queries; they do not by
themselves predict a perplexity number, and they do not claim that every key
quantisation destroys every model. What they establish is that the *mechanism*
of the collapse is structural, that no codebook redesign at fixed cardinality
can remove it, and that the correct axis of improvement is bit width, not format
richness.

**Limits of the measurement.** Three collapsed key formats triangulate the
empirical claim, but they share one implementation family; fundamentality is
carried by the theorems, not by the measurement. The measurement is a single
text slice, a single model and a single context length, and per-arm standard
errors were not captured. The combined $K8/V4$ cell — the arm the analysis
nominates — has not been run.

**Why the prediction was so badly beaten.** The prior prediction was a $\ge 5 \times$ key-versus-value asymmetry; the measurement gave $\approx 2.1 \times 10^{5}$. Sections 5 and 6 explain the gap: the prediction implicitly assumed both
paths were linear with different constants. In fact one path is linear
($\delta_V$) and the other is exponential in an amplified quantity
($e^{2\|q\|_1 \delta_K} - 1$), and then geometric in depth. A ratio of five
would require the two paths to be of the same functional type. They are not.

**Practical summary.** Split the cache budget by role. Keys get at least eight
bits; values may take four. Do not spend engineering effort on richer four-bit
key formats, and do not expect a normalisation scheme to help.

---

## 11. Future work

Three conjectures, each falsifiable and each with a clear route.

**1. A query-norm law for the cliff location.** The critical key bit width $b^{*}$
at which perplexity departs from the control should satisfy $b^{*} = \log_2(\|q\|_1 R/m) + \Theta(1)$, with $m$ the median top-1 logit margin. Corollary 8.3 is
logarithmic in the amplification, so the cliff is a threshold *in bits*: a
doubling of $\|q\|_1$ must be paid for with exactly one extra key bit.
Propositions 8.4 and Theorem 8.6 already bracket the threshold at one scale;
instrumenting a serving stack for $\|q\|_1$ and the margin distribution turns the
bracket into a prediction a single sweep can refute.

**2. A margin-mass criterion.** Perplexity damage should be governed not by the
worst-case margin but by the *mass* of tokens whose margin falls below
$2\|q\|_1\delta_K$: $\Delta\mathrm{PPL}/\mathrm{PPL} \approx C \cdot \mathbb{P}(\text{margin} < 2\|q\|_1\delta_K)$ with a model-independent constant
$C$. Theorem 8.2 is a per-token certificate, so aggregate loss is a measure of
the certificate's failure set, and Theorem 5.2 controls the damage each failed
token can contribute. Only the aggregation step is missing, and it concerns one
measurable distribution.

**3. Depth amplification is architectural, not format-dependent.** The per-layer
amplification factor $\gamma$ of Theorem 6.1 should be a property of the
architecture rather than of the quantiser: the same $\gamma$ (within measurement
error) should fit uniform, scale-and-offset and nonuniform key caches at every
bit width. Theorem 4.8 already shows the codebook shape is irrelevant to the
worst case; the conjecture extends that irrelevance to the observed growth rate.

Beyond these: extend the exponential budget of Corollary 5.5 from a single head
to a full residual stack with explicit constants; characterise the optimal
*non-uniform-across-layers* key bit allocation given per-layer margin
statistics; and test whether the $K8/V4$ allocation predicted by Theorem 7.4 is
quality-free in practice, which is the immediate experiment.

\begin{abstract}
Autoregressive transformer inference caches, for every processed token, a
\emph{key} vector and a \emph{value} vector. Compressing this cache is the
dominant lever on serving cost, and standard practice compresses both halves
identically. We show that this is exactly wrong, and that the reason is
structural rather than empirical.

A controlled measurement isolating the two halves gives a damage ratio of
approximately $2.14\times 10^{5}$: quantising the value cache to four bits costs
$+0.166\%$ perplexity, while quantising the key cache to four bits costs
$+35{,}597\%$. Three distinct four-bit key representations --- a uniform grid, a
scale-and-offset block format, and a nonuniform codebook --- all collapse, with
the richer formats offering no rescue.

We prove that this asymmetry is a property of the attention functional. The
read-out is a convex combination of the values, hence $1$-Lipschitz in the
values with a constant independent of query, scores, context length, depth and
head dimension, and this constant is attained. The key path, by contrast, admits
\emph{no} Lipschitz constant: for every key resolution $\delta>0$ there is a
query and a pair of key caches within $\delta$ whose read-outs differ by at
least $1/4$, so the key-to-value damage ratio has no finite upper bound.
Moreover, for \emph{any} key quantiser whose per-block codebook has at most $N$
entries --- with no structural assumption at all --- there exist two keys at
distance $\ge 1/N$ that it identifies and a query of $\ell^1$ norm $\le 2N$ at
which the read-out error is at least $1/4$; only the cardinality of the codebook
enters, refuting the ``richer format'' hypothesis structurally. The matching
upper bound exhibits the functional form of the cliff: the read-out error is at
most $(e^{2\eta}-1)B+\delta_V$ with $\eta=\lone{q}\delta_K$ --- exponential in
the key resolution, linear in the value resolution. Through depth, the key
recursion is geometrically amplifying and unbounded while the value recursion is
confined to its initial band at every depth; and the governing amplification
$\lone{q}R/2^{b}$ is invariant under key/query rescaling, so no normalisation
scheme can buy key bits.

Under the first-order damage model $D_A(b_K,b_V)=A/2^{b_K}+1/2^{b_V}$, moving a
bit from values to keys strictly helps precisely when $2^{b_K}<A\cdot 2^{b_V}$;

average bit rate and better than the reversed $K4/V8$ by more than a factor of
eight. A margin criterion converts this into a bit count: a $b$-bit key grid of
range $R$ preserves every attention decision of logit margin exceeding
$2\lone{q}R/2^{b}$, which is met at eight bits and provably violated at four at
the same reference scale.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The cache and its cost}

A decoder-only transformer generating token $T+1$ must attend over all $T$
previous positions. To avoid recomputing them, it stores per position and per
attention head a key vector $k_i\in\R^{d}$ and a value vector $v_i\in\R^{d}$.
This \emph{KV cache} grows linearly in context length and, at long context,
exceeds the model parameters in size. It is therefore the first target of
compression, and the standard tool is uniform quantisation: replace each
$16$-bit float by a $4$-bit code drawn from a per-block codebook.

Practitioners have long reported that $4$-bit KV caches are unreliable. The
usual diagnosis is a formats problem, and the usual remedy is a richer format:
add a per-block offset so the grid can translate (a \emph{scale-and-offset}
format), or abandon uniformity for a codebook fitted to the empirical
distribution (a \emph{nonuniform} format). We report a controlled measurement
that identifies a different diagnosis, and a set of theorems that explain why
the remedy cannot work.

\subsection{The measurement}

Held-out perplexity on a fixed text slice (context length $2048$), with a
full-precision control at $7.1093$:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
Arm & Perplexity & $\Delta$PPL vs.\ control \\
\midrule
keys and values, $4$-bit scale-and-offset & $3{,}158.07$ & $+44{,}322\%$ \\
keys and values, $4$-bit nonuniform codebook & $1{,}627.35$ & $+22{,}790\%$ \\
\textbf{keys $4$-bit uniform, values full precision} & $2{,}537.80$ & $+35{,}597\%$ \\
\textbf{keys full precision, values $4$-bit uniform} & $7.1211$ & $+0.166\%$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Three findings. First, block scale-and-offset does \emph{not} rescue the keys;
it is marginally worse than the raw uniform grid. Second, the prior prediction
of a key-versus-value asymmetry of at least $5\times$ is confirmed far beyond
prediction: the measured damage ratio is $35597/0.166\approx 2.14\times 10^{5}$.
Third, the nonuniform codebook ranks best among the three collapsed formats ---
a ranking among catastrophes.

\subsection{The claim}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{The entire cache cliff lives in the keys.} Values tolerate raw $4$-bit
quantisation for free; keys survive four bits in no representation.
\end{quote}

\section{Setting and notation}

Fix a head dimension $d\ge 1$ and a cache of $n+1\ge 1$ positions.

\begin{definition}[Softmax]
For $s\in\R^{n+1}$, $\sigma(s)_i = e^{s_i}\big/\sum_j e^{s_j}$. The denominator
is strictly positive, so $\sigma$ is well defined, $\sigma(s)_i>0$ for all $i$,
and $\sum_i \sigma(s)_i = 1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Attention read-out]
For scores $s$ and a scalar value channel $v\in\R^{n+1}$,
\[
A(s,v) \;=\; \sum_i \sigma(s)_i\, v_i .
\]
We analyse one value channel at a time; since the read-out acts coordinatewise
on the value vector with the same weights, all bounds transfer to the vector
case in the sup-norm.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Scores]
For a query $q\in\R^{d}$ and a key cache $k:\{0,\dots,n\}\to\R^{d}$,
$S(q,k)_i = \sum_{t=1}^{d} q_t k_{i,t}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Quantiser]
A \emph{quantiser} is any map $Q:\R\to\R$ whose image lies in a finite codebook
$C\subset\R$. Its \emph{cardinality} is $|C|$; its \emph{resolution} is
$\sup_x |x - Q(x)|$. A $b$-bit format has cardinality $2^{b}$ per block. No
structure whatsoever (monotonicity, uniformity, affinity, idempotence) is
assumed.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Grid resolution]
A uniform $b$-bit grid covering the key range $[-R,R]$ has worst-case per-entry
rounding error $\res(R,b) = R/2^{b}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Strict top]
Index $i$ is a \emph{strict top} of $s$ if $s_j < s_i$ for all $j\ne i$; $s$ has
\emph{no strict top} if no index is one.
\end{definition}

\section{Values are free --- unconditionally}

\begin{lemma}[A convex combination is non-expansive]\label{lem:convex}
Let $p\in\R^{m}$ satisfy $p_i\ge 0$ and $\sum_i p_i = 1$, and let $v,w$ satisfy
$|v_i-w_i|\le\varepsilon$ for all $i$. Then
$\bigl|\sum_i p_i v_i - \sum_i p_i w_i\bigr| \le \varepsilon$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$\bigl|\sum_i p_i (v_i-w_i)\bigr| \le \sum_i p_i |v_i - w_i| \le \varepsilon
\sum_i p_i = \varepsilon$, by the triangle inequality, $p_i\ge 0$ and
normalisation.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Values are $1$-Lipschitz]\label{thm:valuelip}
For all scores $s$ and value channels $v,w$ with $|v_i-w_i|\le\delta$ for all
$i$, we have $|A(s,v)-A(s,w)|\le\delta$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:convex} with $p=\sigma(s)$, which is positive and sums to
one.
\end{proof}

The content lies in the quantifiers: the bound holds for \emph{every} query,
score vector, context length, head dimension and layer. Nothing on the
right-hand side depends on the state of the model, so value error cannot be
amplified by anything attention does.

\begin{proposition}[The constant is attained]
$A(s,c\mathbf{1}) = c$ for every constant $c$; hence for $\delta\ge 0$,
$|A(s,\delta\mathbf{1}) - A(s,0)| = \delta$. The constant $1$ in
Theorem~\ref{thm:valuelip} is sharp --- and never degrades.
\end{proposition}

\begin{corollary}[Value-codebook damage bound]\label{cor:valuecodebook}
If a value quantiser $Q_V$ has resolution $\delta$, i.e.\ $|x-Q_V(x)|\le\delta$
for all $x$, then $|A(s,v) - A(s, Q_V\circ v)| \le \delta$ for all $s,v$,
irrespective of codebook size, codebook shape, query or context length.
\end{corollary}

This is the theoretical statement of the $+0.166\%$ arm: \emph{resolution is the
only property of a value codebook that can matter}, and every $4$-bit format
already delivers a resolution of order $2^{-4}$ of the block range.

\section{Keys are lethal --- no Lipschitz constant exists}

\subsection{Amplification before the nonlinearity}

\begin{theorem}[Query amplification]\label{thm:amp}
If $|k_{i,t}-k'_{i,t}|\le\delta_K$ for all $i,t$, then for every $i$,
\[
\bigl| S(q,k)_i - S(q,k')_i \bigr| \;\le\; \lone{q}\,\delta_K,
\qquad \lone{q} := \sum_t |q_t| .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$S(q,k)_i - S(q,k')_i = \sum_t q_t (k_{i,t}-k'_{i,t})$; apply the triangle
inequality and bound each factor.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The amplification is attained]
With the all-ones query in dimension $d$ and a key perturbed from $0$ to
$\delta$ in every coordinate, the logit moves by exactly $d|\delta|$.
\end{proposition}

So $\lone{q}$ is not slack introduced by the proof: it is the true gain of the
key path, and it grows with the head dimension and the activation scale. Nothing
analogous can appear on the value side, by Theorem~\ref{thm:valuelip}.

\subsection{The softmax selects}

Write $A_2(a,b) := A\bigl((a,b),(1,0)\bigr) = e^{a}/(e^{a}+e^{b})$ for the
two-position read-out reporting the weight on position $0$.

\begin{lemma}[Tie]\label{lem:tie}
$A_2(a,a) = 1/2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[A gap of $2$ decides]\label{lem:gap}
If $b+2\le a$ then $A_2(a,b)\ge 3/4$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$e^{2}\ge 1+2 = 3$, so $e^{a}\ge e^{b+2} = e^{b}e^{2}\ge 3e^{b}$, whence
$A_2(a,b) = e^{a}/(e^{a}+e^{b}) \ge 3/4$.
\end{proof}

Lemmas~\ref{lem:tie}--\ref{lem:gap} say that softmax is a \emph{selection}
nonlinearity: an $O(1)$ logit error is an $O(1)$ output error. No smoothing
occurs.

\subsection{The cliff}

\begin{theorem}[No Lipschitz constant on the key path]\label{thm:cliff}
For every $\delta>0$ there exist a query $q$ and key caches $k,k'$ with
$|k_{i,t}-k'_{i,t}|\le\delta$ for all $i,t$ such that
\[
\bigl| A(S(q,k),(1,0)) - A(S(q,k'),(1,0)) \bigr| \;\ge\; \tfrac14 .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $d=1$, two cached positions, $k=(\delta,0)$, $k'=(0,0)$ and $q=2/\delta$.
Then $S(q,k) = (2,0)$ and $S(q,k') = (0,0)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:gap} the first
read-out is at least $3/4$; by Lemma~\ref{lem:tie} the second is exactly $1/2$.
\end{proof}

The damage $1/4$ is \emph{independent of} $\delta$: refining the key grid does
not reduce it, because the query rescales the ruler. There is no constant $C$
for which ``key error $\delta$ costs at most $C\delta$''.

\begin{corollary}[The damage ratio is unbounded]
For every $M>0$ there is a resolution $\delta>0$ (namely $\delta = 1/(4M)$) and
a configuration with key perturbation at most $\delta$ whose read-out damage is
at least $M\delta$, while by Theorem~\ref{thm:valuelip} the worst-case
\emph{value} damage at the same resolution is at most $\delta$. Hence no finite
constant relates the two halves of the cache.
\end{corollary}

The measured ratio $2.14\times 10^{5}$ is therefore a property of the slice, not
a ceiling.

\subsection{No codebook rescues the keys}

\begin{lemma}[Collision damage]\label{lem:collision}
Let $a\ne b$ and let $z$ be arbitrary. With the one-dimensional query
$q = 2/(a-b)$,
\[
\Bigl| A\bigl(S(q,(a,b)),(1,0)\bigr) - A\bigl(S(q,(z,z)),(1,0)\bigr) \Bigr|
\;\ge\; \tfrac14 .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$S(q,(a,b)) = \bigl(\tfrac{2a}{a-b},\tfrac{2b}{a-b}\bigr)$ has gap exactly $2$,
so the first read-out is $\ge 3/4$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:gap}; $S(q,(z,z))$ is a
tie, so the second is $1/2$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:tie}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[No codebook of a given cardinality rescues the keys]\label{thm:nocodebook}
Let $Q$ be any key quantiser whose codebook $C$ satisfies $|C|\le N$ with
$N\ge 1$. Then there exist $a\ne b$ with
\[
Q(a) = Q(b), \qquad |a-b| \ge \tfrac1N,
\]
and a query $q$ with $|q|\le 2N$ such that the exact and quantised read-outs
differ by at least $1/4$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Consider the $N+1$ probes $x_i = i/N$, $i=0,\dots,N$. Since $Q$ maps them into a
set of at most $N$ codes, the pigeonhole principle supplies $i\ne j$ with
$Q(x_i)=Q(x_j)$; their separation is $|i-j|/N \ge 1/N$. Take $a = x_i$,
$b = x_j$ and $q = 2/(a-b)$, so $|q| = 2/|a-b| \le 2N$, and apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:collision} with $z = Q(a) = Q(b)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:nocodebook} mention only the
\emph{cardinality} of the codebook. Per-block scales, per-block offsets,
nonuniform codepoints, rotations, learned lattices and formats not yet invented
are all covered, because none of them changes the number of codes. Sixteen codes
is sixteen codes. This matches the empirical picture exactly: the
scale-and-offset format was marginally worse than the raw uniform grid, and the
nonuniform codebook was merely the least catastrophic of three catastrophes.
Contrast Corollary~\ref{cor:valuecodebook}, where the only property of the value
codebook that enters is its resolution --- which every $4$-bit format supplies.
\end{remark}

\section{The shape of the cliff: exponential in keys, linear in values}

\begin{theorem}[Multiplicative softmax stability]\label{thm:mult}
If $|s_j - s'_j|\le\eta$ for all $j$, then for every $i$,
\[
e^{-2\eta}\,\sigma(s)_i \;\le\; \sigma(s')_i \;\le\; e^{2\eta}\,\sigma(s)_i .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The numerator satisfies $e^{s'_i}\le e^{\eta}e^{s_i}$ and the partition function
satisfies $\sum_j e^{s'_j} \ge e^{-\eta}\sum_j e^{s_j}$; dividing gives the
upper bound with total exponent $2\eta$. The lower bound is the same statement
with $s$ and $s'$ exchanged.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Total-variation bound]\label{thm:tv}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:mult},
$\sum_i |\sigma(s')_i - \sigma(s)_i| \le e^{2\eta}-1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $x = e^{2\eta}$. The upper bound gives
$\sigma(s')_i - \sigma(s)_i \le (x-1)\sigma(s)_i$. For the other direction,
$e^{-2\eta} = 1/x \ge 2-x$ (equivalent to $(x-1)^{2}\ge 0$ for $x>0$), so
$\sigma(s')_i \ge (2-x)\sigma(s)_i$, i.e.\
$\sigma(s)_i - \sigma(s')_i \le (x-1)\sigma(s)_i$. Summing the pointwise bound
$|\sigma(s')_i - \sigma(s)_i| \le (x-1)\sigma(s)_i$ over $i$ and using
$\sum_i\sigma(s)_i = 1$ finishes.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Key half of the budget]\label{thm:keyhalf}
If $|s_j - s'_j|\le\eta$ for all $j$ and $|v_i|\le B$ for all $i$, then
$|A(s',v) - A(s,v)| \le (e^{2\eta}-1)B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$A(s',v)-A(s,v) = \sum_i(\sigma(s')_i-\sigma(s)_i)v_i$; bound each $|v_i|$ by
$B$ and apply Theorem~\ref{thm:tv}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Combined KV budget]\label{thm:kv}
If additionally $|v_i - v'_i|\le\delta_V$, then
\[
|A(s',v') - A(s,v)| \;\le\; (e^{2\eta}-1)B + \delta_V .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Triangle inequality through $A(s',v)$, using Theorem~\ref{thm:keyhalf} for the
first leg and Theorem~\ref{thm:valuelip} for the second.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Deployment form]\label{cor:deploy}
In terms of raw cache resolutions,
\[
\bigl| A(S(q,k'),v') - A(S(q,k),v) \bigr|
\;\le\; \bigl(e^{2\lone{q}\delta_K}-1\bigr)B + \delta_V .
\]
\end{corollary}

The key term is \emph{exponential} in the product of the query norm with the key
resolution; the value term is \emph{linear} in the value resolution and carries
no amplification. Halving the value resolution halves the value damage; halving
the key resolution squares the tolerance factor $e^{2\lone{q}\delta_K}$. Every
measured asymmetry is visible in the shape of these two terms.

\begin{theorem}[The key term eventually dominates by any margin]\label{thm:dominates}
For all $B>0$, $\delta_V\ge 0$ and $M\ge 0$ there is $\eta\ge 0$ with
$M\delta_V < (e^{2\eta}-1)B$, explicitly
$\eta = \tfrac12\log\bigl(1+(M\delta_V+1)/B\bigr)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
With $c = 1+(M\delta_V+1)/B > 1$ and $\eta = \tfrac12\log c$ we get
$e^{2\eta} = c$, hence $(e^{2\eta}-1)B = M\delta_V+1 > M\delta_V$.
\end{proof}

Since $\eta = \lone{q}\delta_K$, an arbitrarily fine key grid still reaches this
regime once the query norm is large enough: the key side has no safe resolution
in the worst case, which is why the practical criterion of
Section~\ref{sec:bits} is stated in terms of decision margins rather than error
norms. By Theorem~\ref{thm:valuelip}, the value contribution never exceeds
$\delta_V$, for any $\eta$, any $B$, any depth.

\section{Depth: amplification versus averaging}

A single $1/4$ read-out error would not push perplexity to four digits; the
observed magnitude comes from compounding through layers. Let $e_\ell\ge 0$
denote the perturbation magnitude at layer $\ell$. The key recursion is
\emph{amplifying}, $\gamma e_\ell \le e_{\ell+1}$ for some $\gamma\ge 1$, since
a key perturbation both shifts that layer's selection and corrupts the residual
stream feeding the next layer's query. The value recursion is \emph{averaging},
$e_{\ell+1}\le\max(\varepsilon, e_\ell)$ --- the shape forced by
Theorem~\ref{thm:valuelip}.

\begin{theorem}[Geometric growth of key error]\label{thm:geom}
If $\gamma\ge 1$ and $\gamma e_\ell \le e_{\ell+1}$ for all $\ell$, then
$\gamma^{L} e_0 \le e_L$ for all $L$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $L$: the base case is trivial, and
$\gamma^{L+1}e_0 = \gamma(\gamma^{L}e_0) \le \gamma e_L \le e_{L+1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Key error is unbounded in depth]\label{thm:unbounded}
If moreover $\gamma>1$ and $e_0>0$, then for every threshold $M$ there is a
depth $L$ with $M\le e_L$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Since $\gamma>1$ the powers $\gamma^{L}$ are unbounded, so some $L$ satisfies
$\gamma^{L} > M/e_0$, i.e.\ $\gamma^{L}e_0 > M$; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:geom}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Value error stays in its band]\label{thm:band}
If $e_0\le\varepsilon$ and $e_{\ell+1}\le\max(\varepsilon,e_\ell)$ for all
$\ell$, then $e_L\le\varepsilon$ for \emph{every} $L$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induction: $e_{L+1}\le\max(\varepsilon,e_L)\le\varepsilon$, since both arguments
are $\le\varepsilon$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Separation at depth]
Under the hypotheses of Theorems~\ref{thm:unbounded} and~\ref{thm:band} with key
sequence $e^{K}$ and value sequence $e^{V}$, for every $M$ there is a depth $L$
with $M\varepsilon < e^{K}_L$ and $e^{V}_L \le \varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:unbounded} with threshold $M\varepsilon+1$ and
Theorem~\ref{thm:band}.
\end{proof}

Two elementary inductions, opposite fates: multiplication runs away, averaging
does not. This is the mechanism that turns a per-head asymmetry into a
four-order-of-magnitude perplexity asymmetry in a deep stack.

\section{The bit budget: keys deserve the bits}

\begin{definition}[Damage model]
For an amplification factor $A>0$ and bit widths $b_K,b_V\in\N$,
\[
D_A(b_K,b_V) \;=\; \frac{A}{2^{b_K}} + \frac{1}{2^{b_V}} .
\]
\end{definition}

All arithmetic below is exact rational arithmetic; no floating point or rounding
is involved.

\begin{theorem}[Move a bit to the keys]\label{thm:shift}
If $2^{b_K} < A\cdot 2^{b_V}$ then $D_A(b_K+1,b_V) < D_A(b_K,b_V+1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A direct computation gives
\[
D_A(b_K,b_V+1) - D_A(b_K+1,b_V)
= \frac{A\,2^{b_V} - 2^{b_K}}{2^{b_K}\,2^{b_V+1}},
\]
whose numerator is positive by hypothesis and whose denominator is positive.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Equilibrium]\label{thm:equil}
If $A\cdot 2^{b_V}\le 2^{b_K}$ then $D_A(b_K,b_V+1)\le D_A(b_K+1,b_V)$, so a
further transfer to the keys does not help.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The same identity with the sign reversed.
\end{proof}

Theorems~\ref{thm:shift} and~\ref{thm:equil} characterise the optimum exactly:
transfer bits to the keys until the amplified key term balances the value term,
i.e.\ until $2^{b_K}\approx A\,2^{b_V}$.

\begin{theorem}[$K8/V4$ is the unique optimum at $A=16$ and a $12$-bit budget]\label{thm:k8v4}
For all $b_K+b_V = 12$ with $b_K\ne 8$, $D_{16}(8,4) < D_{16}(b_K,b_V)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Substituting $b_V = 12-b_K$ gives $D_{16}(b,12-b) = 2^{4-b}+2^{b-12}$, a
strictly convex function of $b$ minimised where the exponents coincide, i.e.\
$4-b = b-12$, i.e.\ $b=8$, with value $2^{-4}+2^{-4} = 1/8$. The finitely many
cases $b = 0,\dots,12$ verify the strict inequality.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Role split beats uniform split at equal bit rate]
$D_{16}(8,4) = \tfrac18 < \tfrac{17}{64} = D_{16}(6,6)$: at the same average of
six bits per cache element, $K8/V4$ is better than $K6/V6$ by more than a factor
of two.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[The reversed split is far worse]
$8\,D_{16}(8,4) = 1 < \tfrac{257}{256} = D_{16}(4,8)$: spending the bits on the
values costs more than eight times the guaranteed damage.
\end{corollary}

Here $A=16$ is a conservative stand-in for the proved amplification $\lone{q}$;
a larger $A$ moves the optimum further toward the keys, never away.

\section{How many key bits? A margin criterion}\label{sec:bits}

The worst-case results of Section~4 leave open the operational question: what
bit width is actually safe? The right variable is not the error norm but the
\emph{decision margin}, because what a quantised key cache destroys is a
selection.

\begin{lemma}[Margin certificate]\label{lem:margin}
If $i$ is the strict top of $s$ with $s_i - s_j > 2\varepsilon$ for all $j\ne i$,
and $|s_j - s'_j|\le\varepsilon$ for all $j$, then $i$ is the strict top of $s'$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $j\ne i$: $s'_i \ge s_i-\varepsilon > s_j+\varepsilon \ge s'_j$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Margin criterion for key bit width]\label{thm:margincrit}
Suppose every key entry is stored to resolution $\res(R,b) = R/2^{b}$, and the
exact logit margin of decision $i$ satisfies $s_i - s_j > 2\lone{q}R/2^{b}$ for
all $j\ne i$. Then $i$ is a strict top of the quantised scores.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine Theorem~\ref{thm:amp} (each logit moves by at most
$\lone{q}\res(R,b)$) with Lemma~\ref{lem:margin}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Bit count]\label{cor:bitcount}
$b$ key bits suffice for all decisions of margin at least $m$ as soon as
$2^{b} > 2\lone{q}R/m$.
\end{corollary}

The requirement on $b$ is \emph{logarithmic} in the amplification
$\lone{q}R/m$: each extra key bit doubles the query norm (or halves the margin)
that can be tolerated. This is why the cliff is a threshold in bits rather than
a smooth degradation, and why $8$ is a plausible frontier while $4$ is not.

\begin{proposition}[Eight bits are safe at the reference scale]
At $\lone{q}=64$, $R=1$, $m=1$: $2\cdot 64\cdot\res(1,8) = 128/256 = 1/2 < 1 = m$,
a factor-two cushion.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[Four bits violate the criterion]
At the same scale, $2\cdot 64\cdot\res(1,4) = 128/16 = 8 \not< 2$, so the
criterion fails even for a decision of margin $2$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Four bits provably destroy a decision]\label{thm:fourbits}
At the reference scale there is an explicit two-position cache exhibiting the
failure, not merely the loss of the certificate: take $d=1$, $q=64$, exact keys
$k=(1/32,0)$ and quantised keys $k'=(0,0)$. Then $\lone{q}=64$; the per-entry
error is $1/32 \le \res(1,4) = 1/16$; the exact scores are $(2,0)$, so position
$0$ is a strict top with margin exactly $2$; and the quantised scores are
$(0,0)$, which have no strict top at all. The softmax is handed a tie and the
decision is gone.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[No rescue by rescaling]\label{thm:rescale}
Let $c>0$, and rescale keys by $c$ and the query by $1/c$. Then
(i) $S(q/c,\,c\,k) = S(q,k)$, so the logits and hence the entire attention
output are unchanged; (ii) the key range scales to $cR$, since
$|c\,k_{i,t}|\le cR$ whenever $|k_{i,t}|\le R$; and (iii) the governing
amplification is invariant:
\[
\lone{q/c}\cdot\res(cR,b) \;=\; \lone{q}\cdot\res(R,b).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(i) $\sum_t (q_t/c)(c\,k_{i,t}) = \sum_t q_t k_{i,t}$. (ii)
$|c\,k_{i,t}| = c|k_{i,t}| \le cR$. (iii) $\lone{q/c} = \lone{q}/c$ and
$\res(cR,b) = c\,\res(R,b)$; the factors $c$ cancel.
\end{proof}

So the quantity deciding whether a key bit width is safe is a genuine invariant
of the attention configuration: no normalisation scheme, no per-channel scaling
and no reparametrisation of the key space can buy a key bit. Whatever a
normalisation scheme gains in key range, it loses in query norm.

\section{Algorithms}

\paragraph{Role-split bit allocation.}
Given a total per-element budget $T = b_K+b_V$ and an amplification estimate
$A$, return the split minimising $D_A$. By Theorems~\ref{thm:shift}
and~\ref{thm:equil} the objective $2^{\log_2 A - b} + 2^{b-T}$ is strictly
convex in $b_K = b$, so a single sweep over $b = 0,\dots,T$ (or the closed form
$b^{*} = \operatorname{round}((T+\log_2 A)/2)$ followed by comparison of the two
neighbouring integers) is exact. Complexity $O(T)$.

\paragraph{Safe key bit width from a margin distribution.}
Given $\lone{q}$, key range $R$ and a target margin quantile $m$, return the
least $b$ with $2^{b} > 2\lone{q}R/m$, i.e.\
$b = \lfloor \log_2(2\lone{q}R/m)\rfloor + 1$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:margincrit}
this bit width preserves every decision of margin at least $m$. Complexity
$O(1)$; estimating $m$ from a calibration set is $O(\text{tokens})$.

\paragraph{Codebook-collision audit.}
Given a candidate key quantiser $Q$ as a black box and a probe budget $N$,
evaluate $Q$ on the $N+1$ probes $i/N$ and search for a collision.
Theorem~\ref{thm:nocodebook} guarantees one exists whenever the codebook has at
most $N$ entries, and returns with it the explicit adversarial query $2/(a-b)$
and a certified read-out gap of at least $1/4$. Complexity $O(N)$ evaluations
plus $O(N)$ hashing. This turns ``is this new $4$-bit key format safe?'' into a
terminating computation whose answer is always no.

\section{Discussion and honest limits}

The theorems are statements about the attention functional --- a convex
combination on the value side, an inner product followed by an exponential
selection on the key side --- and therefore apply to any implementation. They
are worst-case statements over queries; they do not by themselves predict a
perplexity number, and they do not claim that every key quantisation destroys
every model. What they establish is that the \emph{mechanism} of the collapse is
structural, that no codebook redesign at fixed cardinality can remove it, and
that the correct axis of improvement is bit width, not format richness.

Three collapsed key formats triangulate the empirical claim, but they share one
implementation family; fundamentality is carried by the theorems, not the
measurement. The measurement is a single text slice, a single model and a single
context length, and per-arm standard errors were not captured. The combined
$K8/V4$ cell --- the arm the analysis nominates --- has not been run.

Why was the prior prediction beaten so badly? A $\ge 5\times$ asymmetry
implicitly assumes both paths are linear with different constants. In fact one
path is linear ($\delta_V$) and the other is exponential in an amplified
quantity ($e^{2\lone{q}\delta_K}-1$), and then geometric in depth. A ratio of
five would require the two paths to be of the same functional type; they are
not.

Practical summary: split the cache budget by role. Keys get at least eight bits;
values may take four. Do not spend engineering effort on richer four-bit key
formats, and do not expect a normalisation scheme to help.

\section{Future work}

\paragraph{A query-norm law for the cliff location.}
The critical key bit width $b^{*}$ at which perplexity departs from the control
should satisfy $b^{*} = \log_2(\lone{q}R/m) + \Theta(1)$, with $m$ the median
top-$1$ logit margin. Corollary~\ref{cor:bitcount} is logarithmic in the
amplification, so the cliff is a threshold \emph{in bits}: a doubling of
$\lone{q}$ must be paid for with exactly one extra key bit. The safe-at-eight
and broken-at-four results bracket the threshold at one scale; instrumenting a
serving stack for $\lone{q}$ and the margin distribution turns the bracket into
a prediction a single sweep can refute.

\paragraph{A margin-mass criterion.}
Perplexity damage should be governed not by the worst-case margin but by the
\emph{mass} of tokens whose margin falls below $2\lone{q}\delta_K$:
$\Delta\mathrm{PPL}/\mathrm{PPL} \approx C\cdot
\Prob(\text{margin} < 2\lone{q}\delta_K)$ with a model-independent $C$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:margincrit} is a per-token certificate, so the aggregate loss
is a measure of the certificate's failure set, and Theorem~\ref{thm:tv} controls
the damage each failed token can contribute. Only the aggregation step is
missing, and it concerns one measurable distribution.

\paragraph{Depth amplification is architectural, not format-dependent.}
The per-layer amplification factor $\gamma$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:geom} should be
a property of the architecture rather than of the quantiser: the same $\gamma$
(within measurement error) should fit uniform, scale-and-offset and nonuniform
key caches at every bit width. Theorem~\ref{thm:nocodebook} already shows the
codebook shape is irrelevant to the worst case; the conjecture extends that
irrelevance to the observed growth rate.

Beyond these: extend the exponential budget of Corollary~\ref{cor:deploy} from a
single head to a full residual stack with explicit constants; characterise the
optimal non-uniform-across-layers key bit allocation given per-layer margin
statistics; and test whether the $K8/V4$ allocation predicted by
Theorem~\ref{thm:k8v4} is quality-free in practice, which is the immediate
experiment.

  "demo": "#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Keys Own the Cliff — numerical demonstrations
=============================================

Self-contained numerical companion to the paper "Keys Own the Cliff: A
Structural Asymmetry in Attention-Cache Quantisation".

Everything here is pure Python (standard library only: `math`, `random`,
`fractions`, `itertools`). Nothing is imported from the paper; every function
is inlined so the file can be dropped anywhere and run with

    python3 demo.py

The seven demonstrations correspond one-to-one to the theorems:

  1. Values are 1-Lipschitz          -- the read-out is a convex combination.
  2. Keys have no Lipschitz constant -- damage 1/4 at every resolution delta.
  3. The unbounded damage ratio      -- ratio 4*M*delta/delta grows without bound.
  4. No codebook rescues the keys    -- pigeonhole collision + adversarial query.
  5. The exponential-vs-linear bound -- (e^{2 eta} - 1) B + delta_V.
  6. Depth: amplify vs average       -- gamma^L versus a fixed band.
  7. The optimal bit split           -- exact rational arithmetic, K8/V4.

Every printed number is computed, not quoted.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core attention primitives (scalar value channel, as in the paper)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def softmax(scores: Sequence[float]) -> List[float]:
    """Numerically stable softmax: sigma(s)_i = e^{s_i} / sum_j e^{s_j}."""
    m = max(scores)
    exps = [math.exp(s - m) for s in scores]
    total = sum(exps)
    return [e / total for e in exps]


def attn_out(scores: Sequence[float], values: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Attention read-out A(s, v) = sum_i sigma(s)_i v_i (a convex combination)."""
    w = softmax(scores)
    return sum(wi * vi for wi, vi in zip(w, values))


def score_vector(query: Sequence[float], keys: Sequence[Sequence[float]]) -> List[float]:
    """Logits s_i = <q, k_i> for a key cache `keys` of shape (n+1, d)."""
    return [sum(q_t * k_t for q_t, k_t in zip(query, k_i)) for k_i in keys]


def l1_norm(x: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """The amplification factor of the key path: ||q||_1 = sum_t |q_t|."""
    return sum(abs(x_t) for x_t in x)


def sup_dist(a: Sequence[float], b: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Sup-norm distance, the unit in which cache resolution is measured."""
    return max(abs(ai - bi) for ai, bi in zip(a, b))


def uniform_quantise(x: float, bits: int, rng_max: float) -> float:
    """Round x onto a uniform `bits`-bit grid covering [-rng_max, rng_max].

    Worst-case per-entry error is res(R, b) = R / 2^b (Definition 2.5).
    """
    levels = 2 ** bits
    step = 2.0 * rng_max / (levels - 1)
    idx = round((x + rng_max) / step)
    idx = max(0, min(levels - 1, idx))
    return idx * step - rng_max


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Values are 1-Lipschitz, unconditionally
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_values_are_free(trials: int = 20000, seed: int = 20260828) -> None:
    """Theorem 3.2: |A(s,v) - A(s,w)| <= ||v - w||_inf, for every s.

    We sample wild score vectors (huge dynamic range, long contexts, extreme
    queries) and confirm the bound is never violated and is sharp.
    """
    print("=" * 78)
    print("1. VALUES ARE FREE:  |A(s,v) - A(s,w)| <= ||v - w||_inf")
    print("=" * 78)
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    worst_ratio = 0.0
    for _ in range(trials):
        n = rng.randint(1, 40)
        scale = 10.0 ** rng.uniform(-2, 3)          # scores from tame to brutal
        s = [rng.uniform(-scale, scale) for _ in range(n)]
        v = [rng.uniform(-100.0, 100.0) for _ in range(n)]
        delta = 10.0 ** rng.uniform(-6, 1)
        w = [vi + rng.uniform(-delta, delta) for vi in v]
        moved = abs(attn_out(s, v) - attn_out(s, w))
        worst_ratio = max(worst_ratio, moved / sup_dist(v, w))
    print(f"  random trials                       : {trials}")
    print(f"  worst observed (output move)/delta  : {worst_ratio:.6f}   (bound = 1)")

    # Sharpness: a constant shift of the whole value cache moves the output by

    s = [3.0, -12.0, 0.5, 40.0]
    delta = 0.25
    exact = abs(attn_out(s, [delta] * 4) - attn_out(s, [0.0] * 4))
    print(f"  constant shift delta = {delta}            -> output moves {exact:.6f}"
          f"   (constant 1 attained)")

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Keys have no Lipschitz constant
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def key_cliff_witness(delta: float) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    """Theorem 4.5's witness at key resolution `delta`.

    Keys (delta, 0) versus (0, 0), query q = 2/delta. Returns
    (exact read-out, quantised read-out, |difference|); the difference is
    >= 1/4 for *every* delta > 0.
    """
    q = [2.0 / delta]
    k_exact = [[delta], [0.0]]
    k_pert = [[0.0], [0.0]]
    a_exact = attn_out(score_vector(q, k_exact), [1.0, 0.0])
    a_pert = attn_out(score_vector(q, k_pert), [1.0, 0.0])
    return a_exact, a_pert, abs(a_exact - a_pert)


def demo_key_cliff() -> None:
    """Refining the key grid does not reduce the damage: the query rescales it."""
    print("=" * 78)
    print("2. THE KEY CLIFF:  damage >= 1/4 at EVERY key resolution delta")
    print("=" * 78)
    print(f"  {'delta':>12} {'||q||_1':>14} {'exact':>10} {'perturbed':>11} {'damage':>10}")
    for delta in (1e-1, 1e-3, 1e-6, 1e-9, 1e-12):
        exact, pert, dmg = key_cliff_witness(delta)
        print(f"  {delta:12.0e} {2.0/delta:14.3e} {exact:10.6f} {pert:11.6f} {dmg:10.6f}")
    print("  The damage is constant in delta: no Lipschitz constant exists.")
    print()


def demo_damage_ratio_unbounded() -> None:
    """Corollary 4.6: for every M there is a delta with key damage >= M*delta,

    print("=" * 78)
    print("3. THE DAMAGE RATIO IS UNBOUNDED (keys / values at equal resolution)")
    print("=" * 78)

    print("  The measured 2.1e5 is a property of one text slice, not a ceiling.")

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. No codebook of a given cardinality rescues the keys
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def find_codebook_collision(
    quantiser: Callable[[float], float], n_probes: int
) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    """Pigeonhole search of Theorem 4.8.

    Evaluate `quantiser` on the n_probes+1 equally spaced probes i/n_probes.
    If the codebook has at most n_probes entries, two probes must collide.
    Returns (a, b, code) with a != b, Q(a) = Q(b) = code.
    """
    seen: Dict[float, float] = {}
    for i in range(n_probes + 1):
        x = i / n_probes
        code = quantiser(x)
        if code in seen:
            return seen[code], x, code
        seen[code] = x
    raise RuntimeError("no collision: the codebook has more than n_probes entries")


def collision_damage(a: float, b: float, code: float) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    """Lemma 4.7: with query 2/(a-b) the exact read-out exceeds 3/4 while the
    collided one is exactly 1/2. Returns (query, exact, collided)."""
    q = 2.0 / (a - b)
    exact = attn_out(score_vector([q], [[a], [b]]), [1.0, 0.0])
    collided = attn_out(score_vector([q], [[code], [code]]), [1.0, 0.0])
    return q, exact, collided


def demo_no_codebook_rescues_keys() -> None:
    """Three genuinely different 4-bit key formats; all three collapse."""
    print("=" * 78)
    print("4. NO 4-BIT CODEBOOK RESCUES THE KEYS (only cardinality matters)")
    print("=" * 78)

    def uniform_q4(x: float) -> float:
        """q4_0-style: a uniform 16-level grid on [0, 1]."""
        return round(x * 15.0) / 15.0

    def affine_q4(x: float) -> float:
        """q4_1-style: a 16-level grid with a per-block scale AND offset."""
        lo, hi, levels = 0.0, 1.0, 16
        step = (hi - lo) / (levels - 1)
        return lo + round((x - lo) / step) * step

    nonuniform_codes = [0.0, 0.004, 0.012, 0.027, 0.051, 0.086, 0.135, 0.203,
                        0.292, 0.404, 0.539, 0.667, 0.775, 0.867, 0.941, 1.0]

    def nonuniform_q4(x: float) -> float:
        """iq4_nl-style: 16 nonuniform codepoints fitted to a heavy-tailed prior."""
        return min(nonuniform_codes, key=lambda c: abs(c - x))

    for name, Q in (("uniform (q4_0-like)", uniform_q4),
                    ("scale+offset (q4_1-like)", affine_q4),
                    ("nonuniform codebook (iq4_nl-like)", nonuniform_q4)):
        a, b, code = find_codebook_collision(Q, n_probes=16)
        q, exact, collided = collision_damage(a, b, code)
        print(f"  {name}")
        print(f"      collided keys a = {a:.6f}, b = {b:.6f}   (separation "
              f"{abs(a-b):.6f} >= 1/16 = {1/16:.6f})")
        print(f"      adversarial query q = {q:.3f}   (|q| <= 2N = 32: "
              f"{abs(q) <= 32.0})")
        print(f"      exact read-out {exact:.6f} vs collided {collided:.6f}"
              f"   -> damage {abs(exact - collided):.6f} >= 0.25")
    print("  Every format with 16 codes fails, for the same pigeonhole reason.")
    print()

def kv_budget(eta: float, value_bound: float, delta_v: float) -> float:
    """Theorem 5.4 / Corollary 5.5: (e^{2 eta} - 1) B + delta_V."""
    return (math.exp(2.0 * eta) - 1.0) * value_bound + delta_v

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Depth: amplification versus averaging
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def key_error_trace(e0: float, gamma: float, depth: int) -> List[float]:
    """Amplifying recursion e_{l+1} = gamma * e_l (Theorem 6.1)."""
    trace, e = [e0], e0
    for _ in range(depth):
        e *= gamma
        trace.append(e)
    return trace


def value_error_trace(e0: float, eps: float, depth: int,
                      seed: int = 3) -> List[float]:
    """Averaging recursion e_{l+1} <= max(eps, e_l) (Theorem 6.3)."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    trace, e = [e0], e0
    for _ in range(depth):
        e = min(max(eps, e), rng.uniform(0.0, max(eps, e)) + 0.5 * eps)
        e = min(e, eps)                       # the proved invariant
        trace.append(e)
    return trace


def demo_depth() -> None:
    """Two elementary recursions, opposite fates."""
    print("=" * 78)
    print("6. DEPTH:  keys multiply (gamma^L), values average (bounded band)")
    print("=" * 78)
    gamma, e0, eps, depth = 1.35, 1e-4, 1e-4, 32
    kt = key_error_trace(e0, gamma, depth)
    vt = value_error_trace(e0, eps, depth)
    print(f"  gamma = {gamma}, e_0 = {e0:.0e}, value band eps = {eps:.0e}")
    print(f"  {'layer':>6} {'key error':>16} {'value error':>14} {'ratio':>14}")
    for L in (0, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32):
        print(f"  {L:6d} {kt[L]:16.6e} {vt[L]:14.6e} {kt[L]/vt[L]:14.6e}")
    first = next(L for L, e in enumerate(kt) if e >= 0.25)
    print(f"  key error first reaches 0.25 at layer {first}; "
          f"value error never leaves its band.")
    print()


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. The optimal bit split (exact rational arithmetic)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def damage(A: Fraction, b_key: int, b_val: int) -> Fraction:
    """First-order damage model D_A(b_K, b_V) = A/2^{b_K} + 1/2^{b_V}."""
    return A / Fraction(2) ** b_key + Fraction(1) / Fraction(2) ** b_val


def optimal_split(A: Fraction, total_bits: int) -> Tuple[int, int, Fraction]:
    """Exhaustive exact minimisation of D_A over b_K + b_V = total_bits."""
    best = min(((b, total_bits - b, damage(A, b, total_bits - b))
                for b in range(total_bits + 1)), key=lambda t: t[2])
    return best

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core attention primitives (scalar value channel, as in the paper)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def softmax(scores: Sequence[float]) -> List[float]:
    """Numerically stable softmax: sigma(s)_i = e^{s_i} / sum_j e^{s_j}."""
    m = max(scores)
    exps = [math.exp(s - m) for s in scores]
    total = sum(exps)
    return [e / total for e in exps]


def attn_out(scores: Sequence[float], values: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Attention read-out A(s, v) = sum_i sigma(s)_i v_i (a convex combination)."""
    w = softmax(scores)
    return sum(wi * vi for wi, vi in zip(w, values))


def score_vector(query: Sequence[float], keys: Sequence[Sequence[float]]) -> List[float]:
    """Logits s_i = <q, k_i> for a key cache `keys` of shape (n+1, d)."""
    return [sum(q_t * k_t for q_t, k_t in zip(query, k_i)) for k_i in keys]


def l1_norm(x: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """The amplification factor of the key path: ||q||_1 = sum_t |q_t|."""
    return sum(abs(x_t) for x_t in x)


def sup_dist(a: Sequence[float], b: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Sup-norm distance, the unit in which cache resolution is measured."""
    return max(abs(ai - bi) for ai, bi in zip(a, b))


def uniform_quantise(x: float, bits: int, rng_max: float) -> float:
    """Round x onto a uniform `bits`-bit grid covering [-rng_max, rng_max].

    Worst-case per-entry error is res(R, b) = R / 2^b (Definition 2.5).
    """
    levels = 2 ** bits
    step = 2.0 * rng_max / (levels - 1)
    idx = round((x + rng_max) / step)
    idx = max(0, min(levels - 1, idx))
    return idx * step - rng_max

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. No codebook of a given cardinality rescues the keys
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def find_codebook_collision(
    quantiser: Callable[[float], float], n_probes: int
) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    """Pigeonhole search of Theorem 4.8.

    Evaluate `quantiser` on the n_probes+1 equally spaced probes i/n_probes.
    If the codebook has at most n_probes entries, two probes must collide.
    Returns (a, b, code) with a != b, Q(a) = Q(b) = code.
    """
    seen: Dict[float, float] = {}
    for i in range(n_probes + 1):
        x = i / n_probes
        code = quantiser(x)
        if code in seen:
            return seen[code], x, code
        seen[code] = x
    raise RuntimeError("no collision: the codebook has more than n_probes entries")


def collision_damage(a: float, b: float, code: float) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    """Lemma 4.7: with query 2/(a-b) the exact read-out exceeds 3/4 while the
    collided one is exactly 1/2. Returns (query, exact, collided)."""
    q = 2.0 / (a - b)
    exact = attn_out(score_vector([q], [[a], [b]]), [1.0, 0.0])
    collided = attn_out(score_vector([q], [[code], [code]]), [1.0, 0.0])
    return q, exact, collided


def demo_no_codebook_rescues_keys() -> None:
    """Three genuinely different 4-bit key formats; all three collapse."""
    print("=" * 78)
    print("4. NO 4-BIT CODEBOOK RESCUES THE KEYS (only cardinality matters)")
    print("=" * 78)

    def uniform_q4(x: float) -> float:
        """q4_0-style: a uniform 16-level grid on [0, 1]."""
        return round(x * 15.0) / 15.0

    def affine_q4(x: float) -> float:
        """q4_1-style: a 16-level grid with a per-block scale AND offset."""
        lo, hi, levels = 0.0, 1.0, 16
        step = (hi - lo) / (levels - 1)
        return lo + round((x - lo) / step) * step

    nonuniform_codes = [0.0, 0.004, 0.012, 0.027, 0.051, 0.086, 0.135, 0.203,
                        0.292, 0.404, 0.539, 0.667, 0.775, 0.867, 0.941, 1.0]

    def nonuniform_q4(x: float) -> float:
        """iq4_nl-style: 16 nonuniform codepoints fitted to a heavy-tailed prior."""
        return min(nonuniform_codes, key=lambda c: abs(c - x))

    for name, Q in (("uniform (q4_0-like)", uniform_q4),
                    ("scale+offset (q4_1-like)", affine_q4),
                    ("nonuniform codebook (iq4_nl-like)", nonuniform_q4)):
        a, b, code = find_codebook_collision(Q, n_probes=16)
        q, exact, collided = collision_damage(a, b, code)
        print(f"  {name}")
        print(f"      collided keys a = {a:.6f}, b = {b:.6f}   (separation "
              f"{abs(a-b):.6f} >= 1/16 = {1/16:.6f})")
        print(f"      adversarial query q = {q:.3f}   (|q| <= 2N = 32: "
              f"{abs(q) <= 32.0})")
        print(f"      exact read-out {exact:.6f} vs collided {collided:.6f}"
              f"   -> damage {abs(exact - collided):.6f} >= 0.25")
    print("  Every format with 16 codes fails, for the same pigeonhole reason.")
    print()

def kv_budget(eta: float, value_bound: float, delta_v: float) -> float:
    """Theorem 5.4 / Corollary 5.5: (e^{2 eta} - 1) B + delta_V."""
    return (math.exp(2.0 * eta) - 1.0) * value_bound + delta_v

def key_error_trace(e0: float, gamma: float, depth: int) -> List[float]:
    """Amplifying recursion e_{l+1} = gamma * e_l (Theorem 6.1)."""
    trace, e = [e0], e0
    for _ in range(depth):
        e *= gamma
        trace.append(e)
    return trace


def value_error_trace(e0: float, eps: float, depth: int,
                      seed: int = 3) -> List[float]:
    """Averaging recursion e_{l+1} <= max(eps, e_l) (Theorem 6.3)."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    trace, e = [e0], e0
    for _ in range(depth):
        e = min(max(eps, e), rng.uniform(0.0, max(eps, e)) + 0.5 * eps)
        e = min(e, eps)                       # the proved invariant
        trace.append(e)
    return trace

def damage(A: Fraction, b_key: int, b_val: int) -> Fraction:
    """First-order damage model D_A(b_K, b_V) = A/2^{b_K} + 1/2^{b_V}."""
    return A / Fraction(2) ** b_key + Fraction(1) / Fraction(2) ** b_val


def optimal_split(A: Fraction, total_bits: int) -> Tuple[int, int, Fraction]:
    """Exhaustive exact minimisation of D_A over b_K + b_V = total_bits."""
    best = min(((b, total_bits - b, damage(A, b, total_bits - b))
                for b in range(total_bits + 1)), key=lambda t: t[2])
    return best

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Tuple


def damage(A: Fraction, b_key: int, b_val: int) -> Fraction:
    """Exact first-order damage of a (b_key, b_val)-bit cache."""
    return A / Fraction(2) ** b_key + Fraction(1) / Fraction(2) ** b_val


def shift_bit_helps(A: Fraction, b_key: int, b_val: int) -> bool:
    """True iff moving one bit from the values to the keys strictly reduces damage.

    The criterion is 2^{b_K} < A * 2^{b_V}: the equilibrium is the point where
    the amplified key term balances the value term.
    """
    return Fraction(2) ** b_key < A * Fraction(2) ** b_val


def optimal_split_closed_form(A: float, total_bits: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Closed-form optimum: b_K = round((T + log2 A) / 2), clipped to [0, T]."""
    b = round((total_bits + math.log2(A)) / 2.0)
    b = max(0, min(total_bits, int(b)))
    return b, total_bits - b


def optimal_split_exact(A: Fraction, total_bits: int) -> Tuple[int, int, Fraction]:
    """Exhaustive exact minimisation over all integer splits.  O(T) work."""
    candidates: List[Tuple[int, int, Fraction]] = [
        (b, total_bits - b, damage(A, b, total_bits - b))
        for b in range(total_bits + 1)
    ]
    return min(candidates, key=lambda t: t[2])

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence


def res(key_range: float, bits: int) -> float:
    """Worst-case per-entry rounding error of a uniform `bits`-bit grid."""
    return key_range / 2.0 ** bits


def logit_error_bound(l1_query_norm: float, key_range: float, bits: int) -> float:
    """Guaranteed logit perturbation ||q||_1 * res(R, b)."""
    return l1_query_norm * res(key_range, bits)


def safe_bits_for_margin(l1_query_norm: float, key_range: float,
                         margin: float) -> int:
    """Least b with 2 * ||q||_1 * res(R, b) < margin."""
    if margin <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("margin must be positive")
    need = 2.0 * l1_query_norm * key_range / margin
    return max(0, math.floor(math.log2(need)) + 1)


def certified_fraction(margins: Sequence[float], l1_query_norm: float,
                       key_range: float, bits: int) -> float:
    """Fraction of observed decisions certified to survive a b-bit key cache."""
    threshold = 2.0 * logit_error_bound(l1_query_norm, key_range, bits)
    return sum(1 for m in margins if m > threshold) / len(margins)


def bitwidth_report(margins: Sequence[float], l1_query_norm: float,
                    key_range: float, bit_grid: Sequence[int] = (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16),
                    target_coverage: float = 0.999) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Full report: coverage per bit-width and the least width meeting the target."""
    coverage: List[Dict[str, float]] = [
        {"bits": b,
         "logit_error": logit_error_bound(l1_query_norm, key_range, b),
         "certified_fraction": certified_fraction(margins, l1_query_norm,
                                                  key_range, b)}
        for b in bit_grid
    ]
    recommended = next((c["bits"] for c in coverage
                        if c["certified_fraction"] >= target_coverage), None)
    return {"coverage": coverage,
            "target_coverage": target_coverage,
            "recommended_key_bits": recommended}

def softmax_two(a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """Weight the softmax places on position 0 given logits (a, b)."""
    m = max(a, b)
    ea, eb = math.exp(a - m), math.exp(b - m)
    return ea / (ea + eb)


def audit_key_quantiser(Q: Callable[[float], float], n_probes: int,
                        lo: float = 0.0, hi: float = 1.0) -> Optional[Dict[str, float]]:
    """Search for a collision witness; return a full damage certificate.

    codebook has more than n_probes entries on this interval.

    seen: Dict[float, float] = {}
    span = hi - lo
    for i in range(n_probes + 1):
        x = lo + span * i / n_probes
        code = Q(x)
        if code in seen:
            a, b = seen[code], x
            query = 2.0 / (a - b)
            exact = softmax_two(query * a, query * b)
            stored = softmax_two(query * code, query * code)
            return {
                "key_a": a,
                "key_b": b,
                "separation": abs(a - b),
                "separation_bound": span / n_probes,
                "shared_code": code,
                "adversarial_query": query,
                "query_magnitude_bound": 2.0 * n_probes / span,
                "exact_readout": exact,
                "stored_readout": stored,
                "certified_damage": abs(exact - stored),
            }
        seen[code] = x
    return None

    """Audit a format advertised as `bits`-bit, i.e. of cardinality 2^bits."""
    return audit_key_quantiser(Q, n_probes=2 ** bits)

<script>
// ---------- deterministic pseudo-random cache -------------------------------
function mulberry(seed){let a=seed>>>0;return function(){a|=0;a=a+0x6D2B79F5|0;
  let t=Math.imul(a^a>>>15,1|a);t=t+Math.imul(t^t>>>7,61|t)^t;
  return((t^t>>>14)>>>0)/4294967296;};}

// ---------- attention primitives -------------------------------------------
function softmax(s){const m=Math.max(...s);const e=s.map(x=>Math.exp(x-m));
  const z=e.reduce((p,c)=>p+c,0);return e.map(x=>x/z);}
function readout(s,v){const w=softmax(s);return w.reduce((p,wi,i)=>p+wi*v[i],0);}
function quant(x,bits,R){const L=2**bits,step=2*R/(L-1);
  let i=Math.round((x+R)/step);i=Math.max(0,Math.min(L-1,i));return i*step-R;}

// ---------- state -----------------------------------------------------------

const el=Object.fromEntries(ids.map(i=>[i,document.getElementById(i)]));

const DIM=16;                       // head dimension of the toy cache
function buildCache(n,seed,qn,contest){
  const rnd=mulberry(seed*7919+13);
  // query with prescribed l1 norm qn, random signs
  const q=[];for(let t=0;t<DIM;t++)q.push((rnd()<0.5?-1:1)*qn/DIM);
  // a common base key: the smaller `contest`, the closer the cached tokens are
  // to each other and the tighter the top-1 race becomes
  const base=[];for(let t=0;t<DIM;t++)base.push(2*rnd()-1);
  const keys=[],vals=[];
  for(let i=0;i<n;i++){
    const row=[];
    for(let t=0;t<DIM;t++)row.push(Math.max(-1,Math.min(1,
      base[t]+contest*(2*rnd()-1))));

  }

const dot=(q,k)=>q.reduce((p,qt,t)=>p+qt*k[t],0);

function render(){
  const kb=+el.kb.value, vb=+el.vb.value, qn=+el.qn.value,
        n=+el.ctx.value, seed=+el.seed.value, contest=+el.tie.value/100;

  document.getElementById("vbL").textContent=vb;
  document.getElementById("qnL").textContent=qn;
  document.getElementById("ctxL").textContent=n;
  document.getElementById("seedL").textContent=seed;
  document.getElementById("tieL").textContent=el.tie.value;

  const keyOnly=Math.abs(readout(sq,vals)-base);
  const valOnly=Math.abs(readout(s,vq)-base);

  document.getElementById("kdmg").textContent=keyOnly.toFixed(5);
  document.getElementById("vdmg").textContent=valOnly.toFixed(5);
  document.getElementById("ratio").textContent=
    (valOnly>0? (keyOnly/valOnly).toFixed(1)+"×" : "∞");

  // decision survival: does the exact top-1 stay top-1?
  const top=s.indexOf(Math.max(...s));
  const sorted=[...s].sort((a,b)=>b-a);
  const margin=sorted[0]-sorted[1];
  const budget=2*qn*(1/2**kb);
  const survives=sq.indexOf(Math.max(...sq))===top;
  const badge=document.getElementById("decision");
  badge.className="badge "+(survives?"good":"bad");
  badge.textContent=survives?"top-1 decision survives":"top-1 decision destroyed";
  document.getElementById("decnote").textContent=
    "margin "+margin.toFixed(3)+" vs. certificate threshold 2‖q‖₁·res = "+
    budget.toFixed(3)+(margin>budget?"  (certified safe)":"  (no certificate)");

  // budget table
  const dk=1/2**kb, dv=1/2**vb, eta=qn*dk, B=1;
  const kt=Math.expm1(Math.min(2*eta,700))*B;
  const f=x=>x>=1e5?x.toExponential(3):x.toFixed(6);
  document.getElementById("dk").textContent=f(dk);
  document.getElementById("eta").textContent=f(eta);
  document.getElementById("kterm").textContent=f(kt);
  document.getElementById("dv").textContent=f(dv);
  document.getElementById("vterm").textContent=f(dv);
  document.getElementById("tot").textContent=f(kt+dv);

  drawWeights(softmax(s),softmax(sq),top);
  drawBudget(kb+vb,qn,kb);
}

// ---------- weight chart ----------------------------------------------------
function drawWeights(w,wq,top){
  const c=document.getElementById("cv"),g=c.getContext("2d");
  const W=c.width,H=c.height;g.clearRect(0,0,W,H);
  const pad=44,n=w.length,bw=(W-2*pad)/n;

  for(let i=0;i<n;i++){
    const x=pad+i*bw, hEx=(H-70)*w[i]/mx, hQ=(H-70)*wq[i]/mx;
    g.fillStyle="rgba(62,166,255,.85)";

    g.fillStyle="rgba(224,82,74,.85)";
    g.fillRect(x+bw*0.52,H-38-hQ,bw*0.36,hQ);
    g.fillStyle=(i===top)?"#ffb454":"#96a0b5";
    g.font=(i===top?"bold ":"")+"12px ui-sans-serif";

  g.fillStyle="#e8eaf0";g.font="13px ui-sans-serif";
  g.fillText("exact keys",pad+18,21);
  g.fillStyle="rgba(224,82,74,.9)";g.fillRect(pad+120,10,12,12);
  g.fillStyle="#e8eaf0";g.fillText("quantised keys",pad+138,21);
  g.fillStyle="#ffb454";g.fillText("gold index = exact top-1",W-230,21);
}

// ---------- bit-budget chart ------------------------------------------------
function drawBudget(total,A,current){
  const c=document.getElementById("cv2"),g=c.getContext("2d");
  const W=c.width,H=c.height;g.clearRect(0,0,W,H);
  const d=b=>A/2**b + 1/2**(total-b);
  const bs=[];for(let b=0;b<=total;b++)bs.push(d(b));
  const logs=bs.map(x=>Math.log10(x));
  const lo=Math.min(...logs),hi=Math.max(...logs);
  const pad=46,bw=(W-2*pad)/(total+1);
  let best=0;bs.forEach((x,i)=>{if(x<bs[best])best=i;});
  for(let b=0;b<=total;b++){
    const t=(logs[b]-lo)/Math.max(hi-lo,1e-9);
    const h=(H-70)*(1-t)+6, x=pad+b*bw;
    g.fillStyle = b===best ? "#48c78e" : (b===current? "#ffb454" : "#39405230");
    g.strokeStyle = b===best ? "#48c78e" : "#39405290";
    g.fillRect(x+bw*0.15,H-38-h,bw*0.7,h);
    g.strokeRect(x+bw*0.15,H-38-h,bw*0.7,h);
    g.fillStyle="#96a0b5";g.font="11.5px ui-sans-serif";
    g.fillText("K"+b,x+bw*0.2,H-20);
  }
  g.fillStyle="#e8eaf0";g.font="13px ui-sans-serif";
  g.fillText("guaranteed damage A/2^bK + 1/2^bV at fixed total "+total+
             " bits  (taller = better)",pad,20);
  document.getElementById("budgetnote").innerHTML=
    "With amplification <code>A = ‖q‖₁ = "+A+"</code> and a total of <code>"+total+
    "</code> bits, the optimum is <b>K"+best+"/V"+(total-best)+
    "</b> (damage "+bs[best].toExponential(3)+"). Your current split is <b>K"+current+
    "/V"+(total-current)+"</b> (damage "+bs[current].toExponential(3)+
    "). Move a bit to the keys exactly while 2^bK < A·2^bV.";
}
render();
</script>
</body>
</html>

<div class="wrap">
  <h1>The Pigeonhole Collision Explorer</h1>
  <p class="lede">
    Pick <i>any</i> key format you like — a uniform grid, a grid with a per-block scale and
    offset, a nonuniform codebook fitted to the data, even a randomly scattered one. If it
    has <code>N</code> codes, then probing it at the <code>N+1</code> equally spaced points
    <code>0, 1/N, …, 1</code> must produce a repeat. Two genuinely different keys become
    the same stored number, and a single query of size at most <code>2N</code> turns that
    invisible collision into a completely rewritten attention read-out. Nothing about the
    <i>shape</i> of the codebook enters — only how many codes it has.
  </p>

  <div class="cols">
    <div class="panel">
      <label>Codebook cardinality N = 2<sup><b id="bL">4</b></sup></label>
      <input id="b" type="range" min="1" max="8" value="4">
      <label>Format</label>
      <select id="fmt">

        <option value="affine">grid with scale + offset</option>
        <option value="nonuniform">nonuniform fitted codebook</option>
        <option value="random">randomly scattered codepoints</option>
      </select>
      <label>Codebook randomisation <b id="sL">1</b></label>
      <input id="s" type="range" min="1" max="30" value="1">
      <div class="cert" id="cert"></div>
    </div>

<script>
function mulberry(seed){let a=seed>>>0;return function(){a|=0;a=a+0x6D2B79F5|0;

  return((t^t>>>14)>>>0)/4294967296;};}

function codebook(kind,N,seed){
  const rnd=mulberry(seed*104729+7),cs=[];
  if(kind==="uniform"||kind==="affine"){
    const off=(kind==="affine")?0.5/N:0;
    for(let i=0;i<N;i++)cs.push(off+i/Math.max(N-1,1)*(1-2*off));
  }else if(kind==="nonuniform"){
    for(let i=0;i<N;i++){const t=i/Math.max(N-1,1);cs.push(Math.pow(t,2.3));}
  }else{
    for(let i=0;i<N;i++)cs.push(rnd());
    cs.sort((x,y)=>x-y);
  }
  return cs;
}
const Q=(x,cs)=>cs.reduce((b,c)=>Math.abs(c-x)<Math.abs(b-x)?c:b,cs[0]);

function softmax2(a,b){const m=Math.max(a,b),ea=Math.exp(a-m),eb=Math.exp(b-m);
  return [ea/(ea+eb),eb/(ea+eb)];}

function render(){
  const bits=+document.getElementById("b").value,
        N=2**bits, kind=document.getElementById("fmt").value,
        seed=+document.getElementById("s").value;
  document.getElementById("bL").textContent=bits;
  document.getElementById("sL").textContent=seed;
  const cs=codebook(kind,N,seed);

  // pigeonhole probe
  const seen=new Map();let a=null,bb=null,code=null;
  for(let i=0;i<=N;i++){
    const x=i/N,c=Q(x,cs);

  }

  const wEx=softmax2(q*a,q*bb), wQ=softmax2(q*code,q*code);
  const damage=Math.abs(wEx[0]-wQ[0]);

  document.getElementById("cert").innerHTML=
    "<div><span class='verdict'>collision found</span></div>"+
    "<div>keys <b class='gold'>a = "+a.toFixed(6)+"</b> and <b class='gold'>b = "+
      bb.toFixed(6)+"</b></div>"+
    "<div>separation |a−b| = "+Math.abs(a-bb).toFixed(6)+
      "  ≥  1/N = "+(1/N).toFixed(6)+"</div>"+
    "<div>both stored as <b class='k'>"+code.toFixed(6)+"</b></div>"+
    "<div>adversarial query q = "+q.toFixed(3)+"  (|q| ≤ 2N = "+(2*N)+")</div>"+
